summary: This document discusses how Control Elements (CEs) in a Forwarding and Control Element Separation (ForCES) Network Element can keep working despite failures. It updates RFC 5810 with new normative text for the Cold Standby high availability mechanism.

eli5.summary: A router has a brain and some hands. This explains how a spare brain can take over if the main brain breaks, so the hands keep working.

questions: forces cold standby vs hot standby
what is the forces fepo lfb
what is split brain in forces
subtitle: How a ForCES router keeps working when its controller fails, from cold standby to hot standby.

tldr.problem: A ForCES Network Element can have several Control Elements but only one master, and the original cold standby scheme leaves failure detection, backup start-up and re-association slow or undefined.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7121 gives new normative text for cold standby and adds a hot standby mode in which the Forwarding Element pre-associates with all backup Control Elements, using a new version 1.1 of the FE Protocol Object.
tldr.outcome: Having connections ready makes switching to a new master relatively much faster. The RFC updates RFC 5810 and is itself updated by RFC 7391.

today: RFC 7121 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5810 and has itself been updated by RFC 7391. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem of CE Failure
sections.content:
In ForCES, a Network Element (NE) is built from Control Elements (CEs), which run control and signaling protocols, and Forwarding Elements (FEs), which process packets as directed by a CE. FEs may know about several CEs, but only one CE is the master controller at any time. The RFC calls this 1+N redundancy. If the master crashes or loses connectivity, a backup CE takes over.

The RFC breaks recovery time into four metrics: how fast the FE detects the CE failure, how fast a backup CE becomes operational, how fast the FEs associate with the new master, and how fast the FEs recover their state. In the original scheme the first three are largely undefined; a human operator could even be the monitor, with detection taking seconds to days. A backup CE need not even be running, and the new master assumes zero state on the FE and starts from scratch.

The RFC sets two goals: to describe the existing cold standby more clearly, and to describe how to evolve it into hot standby to improve failover time and NE availability. The CE-CE interface (Fr) is out of scope.
sections.eli5: If the boss of a team gets sick, how long does it take for a helper to start giving orders? This document is about making that handover quick.

sections.title: Cold Standby as Defined in RFC 5810
sections.content:
This section contains new normative text for the cold standby mechanism of RFC 5810. Only one master CE controls an FE, and the FE connects and associates to only that master. The primary and secondary CEs are configured on the FE and CE during pre-association by the FE Manager and CE Manager.

Behavior is driven by the FE Protocol Object (FEPO) LFB. The CEID component names the current master, the BackupCEs table lists the backups, and heartbeat settings help detect connectivity problems. A communication failure, however detected (by the transport mapping layer or by missed heartbeats), MUST be treated as loss of association.

What happens next depends on the CE failover policy. In mode 0 (the default) the FE returns to pre-association and all FE state must be re-created on any later association. In mode 1 the FE enters a not-associated state and starts the CEFTI timer. It may keep forwarding, cycles through the backup CEs in round-robin order and, if the timer expires with no success, goes back to pre-association and brings its forwarding path down. A master can also change the primary CE with an explicit Config message.
sections.eli5: With a cold spare, the helper is not yet at the table. The hands wait, try each helper in turn, and if nobody shows up in time they stop working.

sections.title: Hot Standby and the FEPO Version 1.1
sections.content:
For hot standby, the FEM MUST tell the FE which CE is master and MAY specify the backups. To support it, the FEPO LFB moves to version 1.1. It adds four datatypes (CEStatusType, HAModeValues, Statistics and AllCEType), two components (read-only AllCEs and read-write HAMode) and one event, PrimaryCEChanged. Since no version 1 component changed, version 1.1 stays backwards compatible with CEs that know only version 1.0, though those CEs cannot use the new HA options.

The ordering of the AllCEs table sets the priority in which the FE tries CEs. In the pre-association phase the first CE in the table MUST be tried first, cycling back to the start until an association succeeds, and the FE MUST associate with at least one CE.
sections.eli5: The hands get a list of every helper, in order, and a small notebook recording whether each helper is ready. Nothing in the old notebook was changed, so old helpers still understand it.

sections.title: How Hot Standby Failover Works
sections.content:
When the failover policy is 1 and HAMode is 2 (hot standby), the FE, after associating with the master, MUST try to connect and associate with all the CEs it knows. It MAY flag CEs it cannot reach as unreachable to avoid continuous attempts.

Backup CEs may issue queries, and the FE answers queries and heartbeats from them. Configuration messages (SET/DEL) from backups MUST be dropped and logged as received errors. Subscribed asynchronous events and heartbeats go to all associated CEs, while packet redirects go only to the master.

When the master is considered down, the FE MUST look for the first already-associated CE in round-robin order. If none is found, it MUST try to connect and associate from the start of the list until it succeeds or the CEFTI timer expires. Once a new master is chosen, the FE sends a PrimaryCEDown event to all associated CEs, then a PrimaryCEChanged event naming the new master.

On split brain, the RFC argues the FE is fenced against corruption because it accepts configuration only from the master CE, so the issue becomes mostly a CE-CE problem that is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Because the hands already know every helper, when the boss drops out they just pick the next ready helper and tell everyone who it is. No waiting around.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The "Logical Functional Block (LFB) Class Names and Class Identifiers" registry gains a new column, LFB version, and all existing entries are assigned the value 1.0. New versions of an already defined LFB MUST NOT remove the previous version entries, and the table SHOULD be sorted by Class ID and then version.

The document also registers the FE Protocol Object, class identifier 2, version 1.1, referencing RFC 7121.
sections.eli5: The official list of building blocks now also records each block's version number, and the new version of the control block is added to it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security provisions of Section 9 of RFC 5810 apply to each CE-FE association, and several CEs on one FE each follow the same procedure. Because the FE initiates the association, a CE cannot start one, and such messages are dropped, which protects the FE from rogue CEs.

Once associated, the FE cannot tell a compromised CE from a malfunctioning one. The CE-CE plane is outside ForCES but could be attacked, so the RFC advises secure channels between CEs, attention to DoS and DDoS from malicious or malfunctioning CEs, and care about split brain. Backup CEs that think the master has dropped should first query the FE's CEID component as a sanity check.
sections.eli5: Only the hands may invite a boss, never the other way around, and they only obey the current boss. A spare that thinks the boss left should ask the hands first.
